metaDescription: Six Cuisinart electric choppers and compact food processors from 3 to 14 cups compared by motor, blade design, capacity, cleanup and which jobs each handles.
expertTake: The Cuisinart Mini-Prep Plus 4-Cup is the best choice for most kitchens because it chops herbs, nuts and aromatics quickly and cleans easily. The Cuisinart CCH-3 3-Cup is the value pick for small jobs. Anyone who regularly cooks for a crowd should skip the minis and buy the Pro Custom 11 Cup or the 14 Cup, which handle batches a chopper cannot. Choose by the job you do most, not by the biggest motor.
introParagraphs: An electric chopper is a small motor under a lidded bowl with a two-blade steel assembly that spins fast enough to mince food in seconds. It is the right tool for onions, herbs, garlic, nuts and breadcrumbs, and the wrong tool for large batches or slicing. Knowing which job you do most decides which size to buy.

This guide covers six models from one maker, ranging from 3 cup minis to full 14 cup processors that also chop. We compare motor power, blade design, capacity and cleanup from the listing specs and general food processing knowledge, and we separate pure choppers from machines that add slicing and shredding.

products.name: Cuisinart Mini-Prep Plus 4-Cup Electric Chopper DLC-4CHB
products.description:
The Mini-Prep Plus 4-Cup is the best balance of size and power. A 250 watt motor spins the blade fast enough to mince garlic, chop herbs and grind nuts in seconds, and the listing says the bowl and lid are dishwasher safe while the base wipes clean. Four cups is large enough for a batch of salsa or a mirepoix.

Still, it remains a chopper at heart. It has no slicing or shredding discs and no feed tube, and dense foods like carrots must be cut small first. Compared with the 3 cup Mini-Prep Plus it holds a cup more, and compared with the FP-5 it does not shred cheese.

Ownership is easy. Pulse in short bursts, never fill past about two thirds, and wipe the base with a damp cloth. The blade dulls slowly with heavy use, so avoid ice and hard cheese rinds. It earns its counter space in most kitchens. Because the bowl is a good size for a standard onion, a quartered onion and a few pulses give an even dice without a mess, which is why it is the model we would put on most counters.
products.bestFor: Everyday chopping of onions, herbs, garlic and nuts.
cons: Plastic body can stain with onion and garlic

products.name: Cuisinart Mini-Prep Plus 3-Cup Food Processor
products.description:
The 3 cup version uses the same 250 watt motor and patented blade as its larger sibling in a 24 ounce bowl. Herbs, vegetables and hard cheese are all fair game, and the body is lightweight plastic with push-button control. It suits small households and quick jobs.

The tradeoff is capacity. Three cups limits batches, and large onions must be quartered or chopped in rounds. Next to the 4 cup model it costs a little less and takes less room, but more tasks need two rounds.

Pulse and scrape down the sides once. Wash the bowl and lid in the dishwasher and wipe the base. It is the sensible choice for a single cook. Because the body is light, it is also easy to pull out of a drawer for a single clove of garlic or a handful of parsley, which encourages everyday use.
products.bestFor: One or two people who want a compact, lightweight chopper.
cons: 3 cup limit needs two rounds for big jobs

products.name: Cuisinart 3-Cup Mini Chopper CCH-3
products.description:
The CCH-3 uses a patented auto-reversing SmartPower blade, with a chop or grind button and an exclusive BladeLock system. Auto reversing means the blade alternates direction so both the sharp edge and the blunt edge do work, which helps grind spices and nuts as well as chop.

As the most basic machine in the lineup, it offers no slicing and a small bowl. Compared with the Mini-Prep Plus it uses a different blade design and button layout, so results feel a little different. For small jobs it delivers good value.

Use short pulses, do not run it longer than needed and wash the bowl by hand or in the dishwasher as the manual allows. It suits spice grinding and herb chopping. Because the blade reverses, a spice mix or a handful of nuts is more likely to grind evenly than to bounce around the bowl.
products.bestFor: Small jobs and spice or nut grinding at the lowest outlay.

products.name: Cuisinart 5-Cup Chop and Shred Food Processor FP-5

specList.label: Storage
specList.value: Blade and disc nest in the bowl

products.description:
The FP-5 is the step from chopper to processor. It has a universal chopping blade for salsas, crumbs and mixes and a reversible shredding disc, and the blade and disc nest inside the 5 cup bowl between uses. The cord stores in the base, so the whole machine tucks away.

Do not mistake it for a full-size processor. Five cups limits big batches, and it has no slicing disc listed. Compared with the Mini-Prep Plus 4 Cup it adds shredding, and compared with the Pro Custom 11 Cup it is far smaller.

Wash the bowl, blade and disc, and store them nested. A small kitchen that wants chopping and shredding without a big machine is the intended home. Because the parts nest, the machine takes about the footprint of a large mixing bowl in a cabinet, which is a real advantage in a small kitchen.
products.bestFor: Small kitchens that want chopping and shredding in one compact unit.

products.name: Cuisinart Pro Custom 11 Cup Food Processor DLC-8SY
products.description:
The Pro Custom 11 Cup is a real processor. A 625 watt motor powers through dense doughs and long shredding runs, and two slicing discs control thickness. A compact chopping and kneading cover scales the 11 cup bowl down for everyday jobs.

The tradeoff is size and price. It is bulky to store and takes time to wash, and it is overkill if all you do is mince garlic. Compared with the 14 cup it is a little smaller and lighter on power, and compared with the minis it handles volumes a chopper cannot.

Wash the bowl and discs after each use and store discs safely. It suits families and bakers who cook in batches. Because the bowl is large, wash it promptly after kneading or shredding, since dried dough and cheese are hard to remove from the corners.
products.bestFor: Families and bakers who need batch capacity and slicing.
pros: 625 watt motor handles dough and shredding
Two slicing discs for thickness control

products.name: Cuisinart 14-Cup Food Processor 720 Watt
products.description:
The 14 Cup is the largest machine in the guide. A 720 watt motor drives chopping, mincing, shredding, pureeing and dough kneading, and an extra-large feed tube accepts bigger pieces of food. On and off/pulse buttons give simple control, and the included accessories are dishwasher safe.

The tradeoff is bulk. It is heavy, takes cabinet space and is more than most cooks need. Compared with the Pro Custom 11 it adds capacity and power, and compared with the Mini-Prep Plus it is a different class of machine.

Store the discs carefully and wash promptly after use. It suits large families and serious bakers. Because it is the largest machine here, confirm the shelf height before buying and keep the discs in a dedicated case.
products.bestFor: Large families and bakers who need maximum capacity.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A chopper like the Mini-Prep Plus or CCH-3 minces and grinds in a 3 to 4 cup bowl. A processor like the FP-5, Pro Custom 11 Cup or 14 Cup adds slicing and shredding discs and a feed tube. If you mostly mince aromatics, a chopper is enough. If you shred cheese and slice vegetables, buy a processor. A good rule of thumb is that if you ever want to shred a block of cheese or slice a cucumber, a chopper will frustrate you and a processor will not. Many cooks own both, using the small unit daily and the large one a few times a month.

The minis use 250 watt motors, the Pro Custom 11 Cup uses 625 watts and the 14 Cup uses 720 watts. More power matters for dough and dense vegetables, not for herbs. A 250 watt chopper is plenty for onions and garlic when used with short pulses. Higher wattage also means more noise and more weight, so do not buy a 720 watt machine for tasks that a 250 watt one does well. For aromatics the lower power is also gentler, which reduces bruising of herbs.

The Mini-Prep Plus uses a patented blade, and the CCH-3 uses an auto-reversing SmartPower blade that alternates direction. Auto-reversing helps with grinding spices and nuts because the blunt side crushes while the sharp side cuts. Standard blades chop faster on soft foods. If you grind coffee or whole spices in the same chopper, expect the bowl to hold the aroma, so keep a second bowl or wash it thoroughly between uses.

A 3 cup bowl is fine for one or two people, a 4 cup bowl handles salsa batches, and 11 to 14 cups handle family and holiday cooking. Do not fill past about two thirds, because overfilling is the most common cause of jams and uneven chopping. Cut dense foods like carrots into pieces of about 2 cm before chopping, because large chunks bounce above the blade and leave uneven results. Pulse in 2 to 3 second bursts rather than holding the button.

The Mini-Prep Plus models list dishwasher-safe bowls and lids with a wipe-clean base. The FP-5 nests the blade and disc inside the bowl and stores the cord in the base. Bigger processors have more parts to wash. A machine that is easy to clean is the one you use. Rinse the bowl soon after chopping onions or garlic, because dried residue and odors are harder to remove later. A little baking soda in warm water helps with stubborn smells.

Cuisinart's BladeLock system on the CCH-3 and the covers on the processors keep the machine from running unless parts are locked in place. This matters because blades are sharp. Always unplug before handling blades and never reach into the bowl while the motor is attached. Check that the lid latches fully before pressing the button. If the machine will not start, the cause is usually a lid or bowl that is not seated properly.

specDecoder.meaning: The motor power. More watts means more torque for dough and dense foods. Do not compare watts across different brands without checking the real use, since design matters as much as power.
specDecoder.watchFor: 250 W on the minis, 625 W on the Pro Custom 11 and 720 W on the 14 Cup.

specDecoder.meaning: The bowl volume. Working volume is about two thirds. Do not fill to the brim, since food needs room to circulate.
A blade that alternates direction so both edges work, helping grind. It is a design that suits spices and nuts better than soft vegetables.
A locking system that stops the blade from running unless assembled correctly. It protects fingers during assembly and cleaning.
An opening in the lid for adding food while the machine runs. It lets you add oil slowly to a dressing or mayonnaise.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 14 Cup has an extra-large tube.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and blade
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 250, 625 and 720 watt motors and the standard versus auto-reversing blades. We also noted that more power is not always better for small jobs, since it can overprocess herbs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity spread
howWeEvaluated.description: We covered 3, 4, 5, 11 and 14 cup bowls, mapped to household size. We checked that each size is recommended only for the jobs it can really do.

howWeEvaluated.title: Attachments
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted slicing and shredding discs on the processors and none on the minis. We counted attachments as a plus only for people who will use them.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cleanup and storage
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed dishwasher-safe parts, nesting storage and number of pieces. We also looked at whether bowls and lids can go in the dishwasher.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety design
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at locking systems and covers that prevent accidental starts. We treated an interlock that blocks an accidental start as a basic requirement.

cards.label: Chopper (Mini-Prep, CCH-3)
cards.text: Small, fast and cheap, with no attachments. Great for aromatics and herbs.

cards.label: Processor (FP-5, Pro Custom 11, 14 Cup)
cards.text: Slices, shreds, kneads and handles batches, but takes space and has more parts.

howToChoose.note: Choose a chopper for small jobs and a processor for batches.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A small bowl and a sharp blade so a clove does not spin on the wall. Dry herbs chop better than wet ones.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The 3 cup Mini-Prep Plus and CCH-3 are ideal, since small bowls keep small amounts in contact with the blade.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You shred cheese, slice vegetables or knead dough. The FP-5 or Pro Custom 11 Cup is the step up.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only mince aromatics. A 3 or 4 cup mini does it for less. Many cooks keep both a small chopper and a large processor.

maintenance.task: Wash the bowl, lid and blade
maintenance.why: Onion and garlic residue stains plastic and leaves odors. Washing right away is easier than soaking dried residue later.
Water in the base damages the motor. Use a damp cloth. Never submerge the base or pour water over it.
Dull blades bruise instead of cut and strain the motor. If chopping takes longer than it used to, the blade is probably dull.
A cracked bowl can leak or fail to lock.
Slicing discs are sharp and should not sit loose in a drawer.

faq.q: What is the difference between a chopper and a food processor?
faq.a: A chopper minces in a small bowl with one blade. A processor adds slicing and shredding discs and a larger bowl. If you are unsure, a 4 cup chopper is the best place to start.

faq.q: Can I chop ice or hard cheese?
faq.a: Avoid ice, which dulls blades. The Mini-Prep Plus lists hard cheese, but cut it small and pulse. Soft cheeses and wet herbs are better handled by pulsing.
Pulse in short bursts and cut food into small pieces first. Holding the button turns onions to puree. Cut food into pieces of about 2 cm first.
The Mini-Prep Plus lists dishwasher-safe bowl and lid. Never put the motor base in the dishwasher.

faq.q: Which size is best for salsa?
faq.a: The 4 cup Mini-Prep Plus handles a typical salsa batch. For large batches use the FP-5 or an 11 cup processor. Bigger batches are easier in a processor.
Only the Pro Custom 11 Cup and 14 Cup list kneading. The minis are not built for dough. Kneading is better in a processor with a stronger motor.
